# 10-palus: sources

Back-test entry `10-palus.yaml`: Palus Finance, more yield on a startup's idle cash (YC Winter 2026). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim. **[author]** marks a choice the public material does not make, kept as small as it could be.

Sources, with the short names used below:
- **HN**: Launch HN, 2026-03-06, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47278980 (the founders' post and 89 comments). A comment is cited as HN/NNN, meaning https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=NNN.
- **YCL**: Launch YC post, https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/PfC-palus-finance-better-yields-on-idle-cash-for-startups-and-smbs
- **YCC**: YC company page, https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/palus-finance
- **SITE**: https://palus.finance and https://www.palus.finance/treasury (read 2026-10-22)

Status today: same customer, a wider offer. The YC page says "Palus is your startup's financial advisor". The homepage now says "The world's most advanced fractional CFO firm" (SITE). The treasury product is still on /treasury.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (actor, segment, roles).** The founder was his own customer:
- "we realized we needed the product for our own startup’s cash reserves, and other startups in the batch started telling us they wanted this too" (HN).
- The co-founder named who it is for: "this product is for startups and SMBs that don't have the time or resources to host a fractional CFO or a full-time finance team" (HN/47283812).
- A sceptic named the two people whose time it costs: "the founder, or an ops person's time" (HN/47297953).
- *Roles.* Keel's B2B shape needs one role that lives the problem and another that decides to buy. At a funded startup the person who moves the cash every month is the one who runs finance day to day (a finance or ops lead, or a fractional CFO). The person who signs where the reserve sits is the founder-CEO. The founders aim their product and copy at founders: "We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652). So `finance_lead` is the practitioner (12 people, Parts 1 and 2) and `founder` is the decision-maker (8 people, Part 3). The same company pays.
- **[author]** The split is mine. At the smallest startups the two roles are one person. That is why one practitioner (Grace Mbeki) passes the job to a fractional CFO, and why the commercial vector is read from founders.
- *Segment*: "Startups and SMBs" banking with "Brex, Mercury, etc." (HN). **[author]** I narrowed it to US venture-backed startups within two years of a raise, to match the occasion the founder describes.

**2. What (the job).** The job is to earn more on the cash without risking it and without switching banks:
- "earn higher yields with a high-yield bond portfolio" (HN).
- "a way to earn more yield on fundraise proceeds without switching banks" (YCC, as summarised from the page).
- Context job **[author]**, worded from these: "keep the money from a raise safe and earning until the company spends it".

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- "The typical startup cashflow pattern is a large infusion from a raise covering 18–24 months of burn, drawn down gradually" (HN).
- "you’re giving up yield to get same-day liquidity on cash you won’t touch for six months or more" (HN).
- The repeated moment is the monthly transfer: "easy to set up rules like ("if my bank balance falls below $X then transfer $Y from treasury")" (HN/47280293).
- **[author]** The occasion "cash decision", the window {3, MONTHS}, Frequency 2 to 3 months out of 3, and Prevalence "Most" (p_60_80) are mine. They follow from "drawn down gradually" (a monthly move), and they match 05-paidly's three-month window.

**4. Which people (comparable group).**
- "Say you (like many startups) use Mercury Treasury, Rho Treasury, Brex Treasury, etc." (HN/47280293).
- "founders who've thought about idle cash management" (HN).
- **[author]** The Importance rivals come from what the thread itself raises:
  - runway: "an extra month or two of runway", HN/47282750
  - safety above the insured limit: the SVB-style worry in HN/47279304 and HN/47279349
  - getting cash back fast: "1-2 business days", HN
  - moving money without mistakes: "no manual reconciliation between accounts", HN/47283812

**5. Who pays.**
- The company pays a fee on its own balance: "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM" (HN).
- The founder decides. The pitch is to the founder's time: "It's a one-time setup that takes five minutes. We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652).
- Buyer and payer:
  - **[author]** The founder's tested item is "Nobody else", which fits the five-minute pitch.
  - "The board" is the one other role on the founder's list. The thread itself puts it there: "I am not sure I would suggest my portfolio companies to risk their treasuries" (HN/47279377). SITE also says the design follows "NVCA startup treasury guidelines".
- Purchase friction:
  - "Diligence on a new provider" comes from "it definitely takes weeks to diligence your company and the offering" (HN/47401784).
  - "A tax adviser's sign-off" comes from "they should talk to their tax advisor" (HN/47282781).
  - "Board approval of the cash policy" **[author]**.

**6. Mechanism.**
- "we built Palus to connect to your existing bank account via Plaid" (HN).
- "Our bond portfolio holds short-duration floating-rate" government-backed mortgage-backed securities, "managed by Regan Capital, which runs MBSF" (HN).
- "Liquidity is typically available in 1-2 business days" (HN).
- "All assets are held with an SEC-licensed custodian" (HN).
- "two buttons and a giant number that goes up" (HN).
- Compatibility conditions, Adoption friction efforts and the Commitment step:
  - The tested condition, "They could wait two days for their cash", is the founder's own claim: "most startups can afford to take on a bit more liquidity risk on their long-term cash (on the order of a couple of days)" (HN/47282907).
  - The commitment step comes from "I'd encourage you to start small, try us out, and grow your position over time" (HN/47280532).
  - The tested effort, "Move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury", **[author]**, worded from "The problem is the treasury product bundled with them, not the bank" (HN).

**7. Price.**
- "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM, compared to the 0.15–0.60%, depending on balance, charged by other treasury providers" (HN).
- "Rho charges a variable rate that peaks at 0.6% for any deposit of $2M or less" (HN/47280707).
- Yields: "we target 4.5–5% returns vs. roughly 3.5% from most money market funds" (HN). SITE now says "targeted SOFR + 1% spread".
- **[author]** Keel's price is a money range over a period, and its ladder stops below $10,000. So I state the fee per month on the reserve the founder's own example uses, $4M to $6M: 0.25% of that is $10,000 to $15,000 a year, so $800 to $1,200 a month.
- **[author]** The cost estimate, $4,000 to $6,000 a month, is the yield given up. The founder says "on $5M, it's an extra $50k-75k per year" (HN/47280107), which is about $4,200 to $6,250 a month, rounded to the range. It counts yield given up, which the registry's meaning allows ("foregone alternatives"). It does not count the 0.15% to 0.60% fee the bank's product already takes.
- **[author]** The hourly rate, $75, is mine: a startup finance lead's salary of about $150k a year, over a working year.
- Ability to pay is derived by code: 13% to 30%, small_share.

**8. Occasions (real accounts).**
- No named customer quote is public. HN is the record: batchmates "started telling us they wanted this too" (HN), one sign-up, "I’ve wanted this produce for years. Signed up." (HN/47283895), and many sceptics. Each respondent below is traced to one of them.

## Respondents

Practitioners (primary link, `finance_lead`):
- Dana Whitfield: HN/47279411 ("we wouldn't want to switch even for a higher yield… the operational burden is more important to us than yield", "about 3.2%"). The $300k transfer is **[author]**.
- Marcus Oyelaran: HN/47279219 (self-directed brokerage, "more paperwork and back and forth", then "click that button now!"). The $3M and August are **[author]**.
- Lena Hofstra: HN/47279349 ("nowhere near juicy enough for me to literally bet the company on") and HN/47279304 (bank-run worry). The Treasuries-only policy and the two banks are **[author]**, after the 2023 bank failures the thread refers to.
- Tomás Reyes: HN/47283895 ("I’ve wanted this produce for years"), with the launch post's "large infusion from a raise". Cash sitting in plain checking is **[author]**.
- Aisha Karimi: HN/47279292 ("business savings accounts not much below this (2.85%) while keeping things safe (FDIC insured)").
- Ben Okafor: HN/47280707 (the fee "peaks at 0.6% for any deposit of $2M or less"). The $1.5M is **[author]**.
- Rachel Lindqvist: HN/47282512 and HN/47283590 (PHC and QSBS: "a bunch of startups are raising $20m on $0 revenue … interest … can easily be the only income").
- Hiro Tanabe (gate No): HN/47279242 ("Startups otherwise are lean and won't hold enough cash to get a meaningful return").
- Grace Mbeki: HN/47283265 ("they might be better suited to deal with a fractional CFO service"). The Slack approval is **[author]**; the YC page (YCC) says the firm is reachable around the clock on Slack (paraphrased).
- Owen Castellano (chip): author's invention, filling a gap: no commenter refuses to say. A chipped story is needed so the reading counts one GUESSED person. It loosely echoes HN/47279377 (an investor steering portfolio companies).
- Nadia Seferović: HN/47286820 ("ask your bank manager for rates on a 30 day deposit account … it appeared in my online banking the next day").
- Kevin Duarte: the launch post ("a mutual fund where your principal is at considerable risk – it had a 9% loss in 2022") and HN/47280944 (the short-term bond fund in "one of the leading startup treasury products"). Moving the loss to August 2026 is **[author]**.

Decision-makers (`link: COMMERCIAL_B2B`, `founder`, Part 3 only, no story on screen):
- Sofia Marchetti: author's invention, filling a gap: the thread has almost no willing buyer. She stands for the founders' own case ("putting $5M into Palus yields them an extra $50k-75k per year", HN/47290584) and the batchmates who "wanted this too" (HN). Her $2,000 a month is the bank's treasury fee.
- Jamal Booker: HN/47297953 ("That 50-75k is more like $5k/month out of what is typically a ~200-400k monthly burn") and HN/47401784 ("it definitely takes weeks to diligence").
- Eleanor Vance: HN/47279349 ("bet the company"); the board having to agree is **[author]**.
- Ravi Menon: HN/47279377 ("I am not sure I would suggest my portfolio companies to risk their treasuries"). The investor who had to agree is his.
- Maya Feldman: HN/47283895 (signed up) and HN/47283356 (liked "a number that goes up").
- Daniel Osei: HN/47283590 ("The probability is Low but the impact for us is massive"). The tax adviser's long sign-off is his.
- Irene Kowal: HN/47279831 ("This should be a hard pass for literally everyone … SGOV") and HN/47279261 ("just put the money in a Bond ETF").
- Felix Brandt: HN/47282750 ("I am willing to take a little bit more risk for a higher return … an extra month or two of runway").

No respondent carries a commenter's handle or a real customer's name (SITE names client companies; none is used).

## Open

- **Relative advantage code.** The registry fixes five advantage codes (fewer_attempts, shorter_time, less_worry, less_help_needed, easier_recovery). None means "more money". I used `less_help_needed` with the founder's label "Higher yield without hiring for treasury". It is the closest code, and it carries the founder's claim of "no need to hire for treasury operations" (HN/47283812). A yield code would fit better.
- **Price period.** Palus prices a share of the balance, not an amount per period. The $800 to $1,200 a month depends on the $4M to $6M reserve I chose. Keel has no "percent of balance" price.
- **Cost estimate kind.** The founder's cost is yield given up, not money spent. Decision-makers asked "what it cost the team last month" will report fees and hours, so Existing sacrifice is likely to read far below the founder's estimate. That is a real finding about this idea, but it is also partly an artefact of the question's wording.
- **Window.** The {3, MONTHS} window and the "cash decision" occasion are mine. Public material has no single trigger moment, only "drawn down gradually".
- **Not checked against the engine.** The file passes keel-e2e-eval's `instructions/corpus.py` loader (bound to the registry) and every rule of `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` but S/C/V. Those three need the `expected` block, which a back-test omits by design.

insights.line: What would have made a difference?

whys.g1: Marcus walked away from the paperwork and monthly transfers, so his answer is about ease too and belongs in the 'Easy and safe' group rather than on its own, though his wish for a better rate inside his own bank makes leaving him out one odd placement rather than a misfiling.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line; all three are straight answers about what would have made a difference.

founder.order_why: The flow runs sensibly from context to problem to solution to sending, but the recency question (4) sits between two screens with the same heading (3 and 5), so the context step looks interrupted and then restarted.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 both ask 'Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.'
founder.missing: Nothing asks what it costs: my 0.25% annual fee on the balance, set against the 0.15–0.60% the bank's treasury product charges. Nothing asks who decides to buy, which is the founder-CEO and sometimes the board or investor, not the finance lead who moves the cash. Nothing asks about the purchase friction a founder faces: diligence on a new provider, a tax adviser's sign-off, and board approval of the cash policy.

PRIMARY.order_why: Part 2 keeps pointing back to 'your last cash decision', but Part 1 never had me describe it; it only asked about my bank and idle cash, so I had to reconstruct it on the spot.
PRIMARY.asked_twice: Screens 4 and 7 overlap: whether Palus fits how things are set up for me, and whether I'd move the reserve out of my bank's treasury, are close to the same question for me, since the treasury is the setup.
PRIMARY.missing: What my last cash decision actually was, such as the $300k transfer, its size and where it went. Also what yield I'm getting now (about 3.2% in the bank's treasury), and how much operational burden versus yield matters to me, which is the real reason I wouldn't switch.

screens.instead: Same question, but I'd have typed: "Higher yield on the reserve, cash back in 1-2 days, without switching banks or hiring for treasury"

screens.why1: Right after I said what it does better, Keel shows the advantage it will test, which is the obvious next check in the solution step.
screens.why2: 'Higher yield' and 'hiring for treasury' are everyday words to a startup finance founder, and the bar is stated in plain fractions.
screens.why3: This is my own claim about my product, and I know the yield gap and the no-hire pitch cold.
screens.why4: The one row joins two benefits (more yield, no treasury hire), so a stranger who wants one but not the other can't tick it cleanly, and my core 'without switching banks' advantage is missing as its own row.
screens.why5: The row and the belief keep my wording, 'higher yield without hiring for treasury', word for word.
screens.instead: Rows: 'Higher yield on the reserve' / 'Keeps our current bank' / 'No treasury hire needed' / 'Cash moves back automatically'; test: for most, their last cash decision would have gone better with it.

screens.why1: Once Keel has what Palus does better, asking what a finance lead has to do to get started is the obvious next piece of the solution, and it is where switching cost shows up for a treasury product.
screens.why2: 'Setup, extra steps or learning' is how I would talk about onboarding a startup onto Palus, and the 25-word limit is clear.
screens.why3: I built the onboarding myself (Plaid link, then moving the reserve), so I can answer from what I know.
screens.why4: The only chip, 'Leave this out of the study', is a fair escape for a founder who sees no friction, and the free-text box takes the real answer.
screens.why5: I typed two steps, but Keel's belief keeps only 'move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury' and drops the Plaid link, though the move is the step that really costs them.

screens.why1: Right after I said what they must do to start, Keel shows me its list of those steps to check and pick one to test, which is the obvious next move.
screens.why2: Plaid, the long-term reserve and the bank's treasury (Mercury Treasury, Brex Treasury) are everyday words to me and to a startup finance lead; the only wobble is the intro repeating the title.
screens.why3: These are the exact steps of my own onboarding: connect through Plaid, open the account in the company's name, and pull the reserve out of the bank's treasury product.
screens.why4: Three distinct steps, each under nine words and in my words; the one I'd most want to add is setting the 'if balance falls below $X' rule, but nothing is wrong or overlapping.
screens.why5: The belief 'Most would move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury' is my point that the problem is the bundled treasury product, not the bank, so it means what I typed.
screens.instead: Keep the three rows and add 'Set a rule to top up the bank balance'.

screens.why1: Right after I checked the three setup efforts Keel wrote, it asks me to pick the one I think will stop finance leads; that is the obvious next step before the test is set.
screens.why2: Plaid, the bank's treasury, the long-term reserve and a treasury account in the company's name are all everyday words to me and to the finance leads I sell to.
screens.why3: I know where my buyers balk: moving the reserve out of Mercury or Brex Treasury is the step they hesitate on, not linking Plaid, so I can answer this from what I have seen.
screens.why4: The three options are the setup steps I actually ask for, each distinct; diligence and board sign-off sit in the buyer's part, so nothing is missing here.
screens.why5: The belief and test, 'Most would move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury', are my words unchanged, and the bar of no more than 1 in 3 saying no is a fair test of my 'start small and move it' pitch.

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out is when I'd decide whether to collect emails from finance leads who want in, and 'start small, try us out' is exactly how I pitch Palus.
screens.why2: 'Pilot' is everyday YC-batch vocabulary, and the hint spells out exactly what respondents see and where I find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want sign-up leads from this study is purely my call as founder, and I know the answer is yes.
screens.why4: Yes or no is the complete choice here, the two options are distinct, and nothing is missing.
screens.why5: My pick of Yes is kept, and the respondent line 'Would you try this for real?' reveals nothing about bonds, yield or my fee.

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs right before the study goes out, after the pilot offer, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but the hint packs video, typing, credits, recording once and text-message delivery into one block, and 'records the voice you pick once for this project' needs a second read to see it means a one-time 400-credit cost either way.
screens.why3: As the founder I can judge which voice my finance-lead and founder audience would take seriously after hearing a 5-second sample.
screens.why4: Two voices with previews are distinct and the default is clear, but the options give only names and audio, with no hint of tone or register to choose from without listening, and there is no 'no video, written only' choice for an audience that may prefer text.
screens.why5: It names my respondents as finance leads, matching my actor, and changes nothing I typed about the idea.
screens.instead: Who should ask finance leads your questions? (Daphne, calm and businesslike, picked for you ▶ / Saskia, warmer and conversational ▶), with the hint cut to: 'Every question is also on screen to read and tap; the voice costs 400 credits once, whichever you pick.'

screens.why1: After choosing who asks finance leads the questions, choosing how they answer is the obvious next step before sending.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but "Daphne Daphne" reads as a glitch and the "catches every spoken answer... more than 9 in 10 where it is loud" line needs a second read to understand it means transcription accuracy.
screens.why3: As the founder I know my batchmates' finance leads are busy and would rather tap through quickly, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: The three options are complete and distinct, but the AI option's text is cluttered with a duplicated name and the inline "Hear her" and status fragments run together.
screens.why5: It says "finance leads" as I typed it, and nothing of Palus's product leaks into the format choice.
screens.instead: How should finance leads answer? — AI interviewer (Daphne asks aloud on video; they talk, type or tap) · Read and tap (they read and tap; speak or type in boxes) · Let them choose

screens.why1: Once the interview is set up, choosing who receives links is the natural last step before sending, and it was not asked earlier.
screens.why2: The options are plain, but in the first one the label runs into its explanation with no separator ('People I know by name I send each one their own link'), so it takes a second read.
screens.why3: I know who I'd reach: my YC batchmates and the founders and finance leads I talk to, so I can answer from my own situation.
screens.why4: Known people, a Keel-sourced list, and an open link posted in a group (e.g. the YC Bookface or a founder Slack) cover my real ways of reaching finance leads, and they are distinct.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product's meaning is changed here; it is only about distribution, and my pick of named people is kept.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? — People I know by name: I send each one their own link / People I found with Keel: from a Contacts search, Keel makes a link for each / A group, with one open link: I post it where finance leads already are, and each signs in with Google

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits in the verdict line beside its deciding number, Relative advantage at 2 of 5, and the card adds the bar of 4 of 5, so I know which belief sank it and by how much (though Adoption friction also failed and only shows on its card)
screens.why_b2: There is no chart, but the per-card counts and bars are there; still, the denominators shift (6, 5, 6 of 7 answered) with no reason given, and Relative advantage's '3 short of it' beside '2 short' made me read it twice to see one is people short of my claim and the other people short of the bar
screens.why_b3: All three names and belief lines are word for word what I checked: two days' wait, higher yield without hiring for treasury, and moving the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what two failed beliefs mean for Palus, such as that founders don't see the yield gain on their last cash decision, or that half won't leave the bank's treasury, so I have to work out the next move myself
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 and each denominator are visible, but the page never says 7 is a small sample, and Adoption friction is called flatly 'did not hold' when one more yes would have flipped it
screens.instead: Did not hold on two of three: only 2 of 5 say their last cash decision would have gone better and 3 of 6 would move the reserve, each one or two people short of the bar among only 7 who answered, so the wait is fine but the yield gain isn't landing; open Relative advantage to see what the 3 said instead.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits beside "6 of 6 said yes, easily or most of the time · bar 4 of 6", so I see the verdict and the deciding number together.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answer choices over 6 counted people, and the strip shows all 6 cells for me with the marker at 4, so what is counted, out of how many and where the bar sits are plain at once.
screens.why_b3: The title is Compatibility and the belief is "For most finance leads, they could wait two days for their cash", word for word what I checked.
screens.why_b4: Pointing me to adoption friction gives me a direction, but the stage page told me relative advantage is what failed, and this line doesn't square the two or say what to do about the two-day wait.
screens.why_b5: The count line honestly says "a small group: a lean, not a call", but the So line says the two-day wait "is not what will stop them" when the question asked about fitting their setup, not about waiting two days for cash.
screens.instead: 6 of 6 said Palus would have fitted how their last cash decision was set up, though that is a lean from a small group, not proof the two-day wait is fine; what failed is relative advantage (2 of 5), so fix the case for switching before the setup.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside "2 of 5 said it would have gone better · bar 4 of 5 · 2 short", so I know the verdict and the count that decides it, though "2 at or beyond what you said, 3 short of it" is awkward wording for a yes/no answer.
screens.why_b2: Better 2 (all "a lot") against Same 3 over 5 counted is plain at a glance, but the bar given both as "4 of 5" and as "no more than 1 in 3" made me stop and do the arithmetic to see they match.
screens.why_b3: The title and belief line are word for word what I checked: "For most, their last cash decision would have gone better with it: higher yield without hiring for treasury."
screens.why_b4: "Their reasons are below and on the Insights tab" sends me elsewhere instead of saying what the three no-difference answers have in common: two-click access to cash, no new paperwork, and insured over yield, which means my yield pitch is not the advantage these finance leads value.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (7 answered, 5 counted, with Lena and Rachel's exclusions named), the screen flags "a small group: a lean, not a call", and it says the question was hypothetical, so nothing is claimed beyond the five.
screens.instead: Did not hold: 2 of 5 would have done better, 3 saw no difference (you allowed 1). All three valued same-day access, no extra paperwork or insured safety over more yield, so lead with access and safety, not the rate. A lean from 5, not a call.

screens.why_b1: The card says 'Did not hold' with '3 of 6 would do it · bar 4 of 6 · 1 short' beside it, so I know the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The chart shows the four answers among the 6 counted, plus a strip of 3 for and 3 against with the marker at 4, so what is counted, over how many and where the bar sits read at first look.
screens.why_b3: The title is Adoption friction and the line is word for word what I checked: 'Most would move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury.'
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the count and says 'their reasons are below', but only one quote follows, the tax-break one, so it never says what this means for my pitch (start small, the ops burden, tax-ready cash).
screens.why_b5: n stays visible (7 answered, 6 counted, Lena left out as a guess), the conditional yes is flagged and 'a lean, not a call' is said; the switch to 'your bar of 2' in the So line is confusing but not an overstatement.
screens.instead: 3 of 6 would not move the reserve, one short of your bar of 4 of 6. The no's cite the operational burden and keeping cash plain for tax, so pitch a small first move and a tax-safe setup before asking for the whole reserve.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its status word (Did not hold / Holding up), with the deciding count and bar right beside it: 2 of 5 against a bar of 4, 3 of 6 against 4, and 6 of 6 against 4.
screens.why_b3: Relative advantage, Adoption friction and Compatibility carry the exact belief lines I checked: higher yield without hiring for treasury, moving the long-term reserve, and waiting two days.
screens.why_b4: The 'Easy and safe, not a bit more yield' theme hints that my yield pitch is the wrong lead, but nothing on the screen says what to change, such as leading on insurance, explainability and staying inside the bank, or sizing a small first move.
screens.why_b5: Nothing overclaims, but n of 5 and 6 is never called small, and the Compatibility box is confusing: it says 6 of 6 held, labels a group 'On their own (1)', then shows Lena's 'Only sometimes' quote as not counted, and the quote is about the board and insurance rather than the two-day wait.
screens.why_b6: The quotes teach me what I did not type: 'nobody asks why we earned a bit less, they'd ask why we lost any', paying bills out of treasury every month, wanting a better rate inside the bank I already use, and an accountant wanting plain cash for the tax break.

screens.why1: As a first screen it makes sense to check where we bank before asking me about how we park our raise money, because the study is plainly about startups on Mercury, Brex and the like.
screens.why2: Mercury and Brex are everyday names to me, but 'or similar' makes me stop and wonder whether it means fintech banking apps only or also counts our JPMorgan or First Citizens account.
screens.why3: I know exactly where our accounts sit because I log into them every day.
screens.why4: Yes and No covers most cases, but there is no clean answer for the common setup where we keep operating cash on Mercury and the rest of the raise at a big bank or in treasuries, so 'Yes' and 'No' could both be true.
screens.why5: Nothing about the product leaks, but the screener only checks the bank and drops the part about having raised in the last two years and holding that cash, so the gate is looser than the founder's segment.
screens.why6: Heard aloud it is one short question with a yes or no, though 'I'll read 2 options' is a little stiff for a yes or no.
screens.instead: Does your company keep cash from its last raise at Mercury, Brex or another startup-focused bank? Yes; No, only at a traditional bank.

screens.why1: Right after confirming we bank with Mercury, asking whether any of the raise sat earning nothing is the obvious next screen for how I park cash.
screens.why2: Cash from the raise and earning no interest are exactly how I talk about our checking versus treasury balances.
screens.why3: I know which of our accounts pay interest and which don't, so I can answer this straight away.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but a gate should carry no escape chip, 'I'd rather not say' is not an allowed escape, and 'I can't recall one particular cash decision' doesn't answer a yes-or-no about idle cash.
screens.why5: It stays on keeping the raise earning until it is spent, and nothing about a product or the founder's terms reaches me.
screens.why6: It is one short question ending in 'Yes or no', easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: In the last 3 months, did any of the cash from your raise earn no interest? Yes · No (no escape chip)

screens.why1: Right after asking whether any of my raise cash sat earning nothing, showing me something that would put it to work is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Plaid, treasury account, floating-rate and government-backed mortgage bonds are all words I use, but 'the long-term reserve' assumes I already split my cash that way when I'd just say the cash we won't touch for a year or more.
screens.why3: Where the raise sits, what it earns and how fast I can pull it back to checking is my job every week.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: The idea comes through as intended, but 'the long-term reserve' reads as the founder's own framing slipped in undefined, as if it were already my category.
screens.why6: It runs to six sentences instead of three lines, and 'short-duration, floating-rate, government-backed mortgage bonds' is a mouthful to hold on one hearing.
screens.instead: Imagine Palus, a treasury account for cash you won't need for a while. It links to your bank, invests that cash in short-term government-backed bonds held in your company's name, and gets it back to checking in one to two business days. The people building it believe it would earn about 4.5 to 5 percent.

screens.why1: Right after the Palus card, asking whether it would fit how my cash is set up is the obvious first question about the idea.
screens.why2: 'My last cash decision' and 'the way things were set up' are vague: I can't tell if it means our Mercury accounts, our board-approved investment policy, sign-off on transfers, or how fast we need the money back, and 'it' leaves me guessing whether that means Palus or the decision.
screens.why3: I know our setup cold, Mercury, the policy, who approves moving $300k, but I'd be guessing how a managed bond account works with it, and the question doesn't say which part of the setup to check.
screens.why4: The question is about one past decision, but 'Yes, most of the time' and 'Only sometimes' are frequency answers that don't fit a single occasion; 'No' and the escape work.
screens.why5: The card keeps the idea in plain trade words, but the question has lost whatever specific condition the founder meant to check (liquidity timing, policy, approvals) and become a generic 'would it fit'.
screens.why6: Short, one question, and four short options I can hold when I hear them once, with the escape said last.
screens.instead: Could you have moved the raise's cash into Palus under the investment policy and approvals you had then? Yes; yes, with some steps; or no. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether it would have fitted how we're set up, asking whether it would have made the decision go better is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: "Managed bond treasury account" is plain to me, but "your last cash decision" is vague (where we parked the raise? a sweep change? moving $300k?), and "better" doesn't say whether it means yield or operational burden, which for me pull in opposite directions.
screens.why3: I made the call on where our raise cash sits and why we stayed put, so I can judge an alternative against it from my own experience.
screens.why4: The scale is complete and distinct, a plain "Worse" covers my likely answer since more moving parts would be worse for us, and "I can't tell" fits a hypothetical.
screens.why5: Only the idea card's own name and one-line description reach me, and the question doesn't push any further claim about the product.
screens.why6: One short balanced question and four short options, easy to hold, with the escape said last in one breath.
screens.instead: Think of where you decided to keep the cash from your raise. Would Palus have made that go better for you, all things counted, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: Following up on my answer that Palus wouldn't change much is the obvious next thing to ask me, and it fits as the last screen.
screens.why2: I had to read 'until the company sends it' twice, because we spend that money rather than send it, and the whole phrase is stiffer than how I'd say it ('our cash from the raise').
screens.why3: I run our accounts day to day, so I know what would make holding the raise less work for me, mostly less operational hassle rather than a bit more yield.
screens.why4: It is a free-text box with no options.
screens.why5: 'Sends it' has drifted from 'spends it' and changes the sense a little, though nothing of the product leaks beyond the Palus name already shown on the idea card.
screens.why6: Said aloud, it runs about 30 words, and the long 'keeping the money from a raise safe and earning until the company sends it' clause is a mouthful to hold in one hearing.
screens.instead: You said Palus wouldn't make much difference. What would make looking after your raise cash easier for you, if anything?

screens.why1: After asking whether Palus would have fitted and whether it would have helped, asking whether I'd actually move the reserve out of Mercury Treasury is the obvious last question about the switch itself.
screens.why2: Long-term reserve and the bank's treasury are how I talk about our cash, so I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: We do keep the raise in our bank's treasury at about 3.2%, and whether I'd move it is my call to make, so I can answer it from what I do.
screens.why4: The scale is lopsided: it has a qualified yes and a probably not but no plain probably yes, and Yes, if it was clearly worth it is close to what a reluctant yes would also say, though my true answer, probably not because of the operational burden, is there.
screens.why5: It names only what the idea card already shows on purpose, a managed bond treasury account that means moving the reserve, with no leak of the founder's plan or roles.
screens.why6: One short question, a list of four I can hold, and the one escape said last, with nothing that reads badly aloud.
screens.instead: To use Palus, you'd move your long-term reserve out of your bank's treasury. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Probably yes · Probably not · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: I just said I wouldn't move the reserve, so asking what stops me is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: Long-term reserve and the bank's treasury are words I use every week; Mercury Treasury is literally where our cash sits.
screens.why3: I know exactly why: another account means more logins, more approvals and more reconciling, and that operational burden matters more to us than a bit of yield.
screens.why4: It is a free-text box with no options.
screens.why5: It assumes 'too much trouble' is my reason, when someone else might say no because of risk or yield, so it drifts slightly from a neutral 'why not'.
screens.why6: One short question with no list, easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: What would stop you moving the long-term reserve out of your bank's treasury, if anything?
